I have been farming these eight mu of land in Quzhou for over forty years, and I know what works here. Everyone in our village grows winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots — it is the only system that makes sense with our soil, water, and climate. I am fifty-eight now, I never went to school, and I do not have the strength or the knowledge to gamble on vegetables or cotton like some younger farmers try. Wheat and maize are safe: the government gives subsidies for wheat, the machinery can be hired easily, and I understand every step of the cycle. 

For this year, my winter wheat is already in the ground — I sowed it last October using Luyuan 502, an improved variety that has given me good harvests before. I will rotary till the soil before the next wheat sowing, but for the summer maize I will plant directly into the wheat stubble without any tillage; that is how we have done it for years now, and it saves time and diesel. I will put plenty of urea and compound fertilizer on the wheat — about forty kilograms of nitrogen per mu, with a little phosphate — and topdress it at green-up and jointing. The maize will get less fertilizer, around fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu, mostly at planting and when it is knee-high. I will irrigate the wheat four times: winter irrigation, green-up, jointing, and grain filling. The maize only needs two good irrigations, at the big trumpet leaf stage and during grain filling. I will spray pesticides four times on the wheat and three times on the maize — herbicide once, and insecticide and fungicide as needed when I see problems. I expect about 550 kilograms per mu from the wheat and 560 kilograms per mu from the maize if the weather holds.
